stories.headline: Murasu cyclone disrupts flight services at Vijayawada airport
stories.title: Murasu cyclone disrupts flight services at Vijayawada airport
stories.summary: IndiGo cancels eight flights scheduled for November 3
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Vijayawada: Cyclone Murasu has disrupted flight operations at Vijayawada International Airport at Gannavaram, with several services cancelled on Monday and Tuesday (November 3), causing inconvenience to passengers travelling to various destinations.
IndiGo has cancelled eight flight operations scheduled for Tuesday (November 3) to and from Vijayawada as a precautionary measure in view of the cyclone.

According to information shared by the Airport officials, the cancellations include seven domestic services and one international flight, affecting connectivity with Delhi, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, Kadapa and Singapore.

Among the cancelled morning services are the Delhi-Vijayawada-Delhi flight (6E 6446/6447), scheduled to arrive at 7.25 am and depart at 7.55 am, and the Bengaluru-Vijayawada-Bengaluru service (6E 7203/7204), scheduled between 7.30 am and 7.55 am.
The Hyderabad service (6E 2572/2573), scheduled to arrive at 8.15 am and depart at 8.45 am, and the Chennai flight (6E 7303/7304), scheduled between 8.30 am and 9 am, have also been cancelled.
The international Singapore service (6E 1030/1029), scheduled to arrive at 7.55 am and depart at 9.40 am, has also been called off.
The cancellations will continue through the afternoon and evening.

The Hyderabad service (6E 6326/6327), scheduled between 1.15 pm and 1.45 pm, the Kadapa-Vijayawada-Kadapa flight (6E 7711/7712), scheduled between 2.30 pm and 2.50 pm, and the evening Bengaluru service (6E 7223/7224), scheduled to arrive at 5.25 pm and depart at 5.45 pm, have also been cancelled.
The flight disruptions have affected passengers travelling for business, official work, education, medical treatment and onward domestic and international connections.
Passengers have been advised to check their flight status with the respective airlines before leaving for the airport and contact airline authorities regarding rescheduling and refunds.
Normal flight operations will depend on improvement in weather conditions and the assessment of the aviation authorities.

stories.headline: Maharashtra sets up drought mitigation panel, approves ₹291.91 crore relief for flood-hit farmers
stories.title: Maharashtra sets up drought mitigation panel, approves ₹291.91 crore relief for flood-hit farmers
stories.summary: The measures follow deficient rainfall in parts of Maharashtra during 2026, prompting the government to declare drought in talukas identified under the Kharif season’s Trigger-1 assessment
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Maharashtra government on Monday (November 1, 2026) announced measures to address drought and flood-related agricultural distress across the State, constituting a high-level committee headed by the Chief Minister to oversee soil and water conservation projects in drought-affected areas and approving ₹291.91 crore in financial assistance for farmers affected by heavy rainfall and flooding between June and August 2026.

Soil and Water Conservation Minister Sanjay Rathod said the committee would monitor conservation projects undertaken through non-governmental organisations, including Paani Foundation and Chandra Foundation, as part of the state’s drought mitigation efforts.
The government has also decided to revive Paani Foundation’s Water Cup competition to encourage community participation in water conservation.
The measures follow deficient rainfall in parts of Maharashtra during 2026, prompting the government to declare drought in talukas identified under the Kharif season’s Trigger-1 assessment.

According to a government resolution issued on November 2, all Deputy Chief Ministers will serve as co-chairpersons of the high-level committee, which will include ministers from departments such as agriculture, water resources, rural development and employment guarantee.
A separate executive committee, chaired by the Principal Secretary of the Water Resources Department, will coordinate implementation and meet at least once a month.
Progress will be monitored using geographical information systems (GIS), satellite imagery, mobile-based monitoring systems and online dashboards.

Meanwhile, Relief and Rehabilitation Minister Makarand Jadhav Patil announced that the government had sanctioned ₹262.70 crore for crop damage affecting 3,09,289 farmers across six revenue divisions, including Pune, Nagpur, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, Amravati, Konkan and Nashik.
An additional ₹29.21 crore has been approved for damage to agricultural land covering 7,675.40 hectares belonging to 34,984 farmers.
The assistance will cover eligible restoration work, including the removal of sand, silt and salt deposits caused by flooding.

Crop damage compensation will be transferred directly to eligible farmers’ bank accounts, while small and marginal landowners will receive assistance for damaged agricultural land up to a maximum of two hectares, in accordance with prescribed norms.
The government has also directed district collectors to ensure that banks do not divert disaster relief payments towards loan repayments or other recoveries.

stories.headline: ICG report on J&K
stories.title: ICG report on J&K
stories.summary: Things should not have come to this pass: foreigners assessing our state of affairs and suggesting what is the way out, because somewhere down the line we shied away from rising to the occasion. The International Crisis Group (ICG) in its latest report “A Trigger in Jammu and Kashmir: Militant Violence under Indian Central rule”, has pointed out certain fault lines while scripting a roadmap for lasting peace. Foreigners have their own way of interpreting things. They see certain things which we are not able to see or express for the reasons better known to us – we are motivated by two considerations that we should be avoiding the high risk areas, and wait for others to speak for us. This doesn’t undermine some of the crucial points in the ICG report. This has captured the reality that reversed the ugly reality of the times before the August 5, 2019 decisions – the abrogation of Article 370, Article 35 A and the announcement of the Reorganization of the state of Jammu and Kashmir that India could retain after the 1948 ceasefire – a journey from extreme terror violence and street protests to the taste of the normal times. Some of the fundamentals scripted in the report are worth looking at with a clear lens, and see where it resonates with the reality and the narrative of Delhi, and tricolour upholding crowds signaling shift in their attitude and approach. The report revolves around three major points – (a) August 5, 2019, perception and reality of peace in Kashmir, (b) Pahalgam attack and the aftermath and call for the restoration of statehood, and (c) dialogue with Pakistan to start with back channel diplomacy with the help of the friendly countries. It is important to understand why Article 370 was abrogated. The foreign think tanks have their own ideas, because they have always invested in their thinking that nothing can happen in Jammu and Kashmir unless there is some kind of third party intervention. The Pahalgam attack of April 22, 2025 that triggered heightened Indo-Pak tensions and 87-hour war from May 7 to 10, has assumed a global dimension. Primarily, the perpetrators of this gruesome attack in which 25 tourists and a local Kashmiri were killed, wanted to place Kashmir in the international spotlight as a place where terrorism continues to manifest the frustration and anger. These elements forgot that Kashmir had changed, they never wanted the revival of the violence. They revolted against terrorists and their patrons in an unprecedented way, sending a clear message to them that they will rise against acts of terror, and this was also a loud shout out about themselves that they were against terrorists and willing partners in the peace-building measures of Government of India. The underlined meaning was that the attack, sponsored and executed by non-Kashmiris, should neither disrupt the narrative nor the promises pledged by Delhi to J&K. Pakistan’s audacity was punished with the launch of Operation Sindoor, and less than a month after the conclusion of the brief war, Kashmir was connected via rail to the rest of country – more than century-old dream became a reality. While the security aspect was taken care of, the public dialogue and the promises were kept on waiting list. The waiting list status has not changed and that has created different type of resentment that remains unexpressed. The ICG or for that matter all foreign elements come as observers and make reports to highlight what suits their narrative, though it must be acknowledged that the balance between the positives and negatives should never be overlooked. There is always something to learn. But it would have been far better had the things that J&K hoped for come its way in the natural course. The ICG has noted it in its critical analysis with an advice to Pakistan: “If it is to convince India that its efforts are genuine, Pakistan will need to aggressively enforce its ban on anti-Indian jihadist groups”, and for India , the report has stated that , “India, for its part, should rethink its stance that Operation Sindoor has only been paused, as Modi has put it, implying that military action could immediately resume if another terrorist attack occurs. While this novel approach is meant to boost India’s deterrence, it puts India on a perpetual war footing and increases the risk of conflict with Pakistan, the consequences of which could be calamitous” In its to do list in the way forward, the report has made an audacious suggestion: “Foreign governments that enjoy friendly relations with both parties, such as the U.S., the UK, EU member states, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other Gulf countries, can also help stabilize the relationship. Considering India’s sensitivities regarding foreign interference or mediation on the Kashmir issue, external powers should move cautiously with quiet, behind-the-scenes diplomacy. They should emphasise that it is in New Delhi and Islamabad’s mutual interest to ensure a sustainable peace in South Asia, encouraging them to use high-level back channels to defuse potential conflict triggers.” This suggestion should be taken with a fistful of salt, and it would be better if the public dialogue is opened with the people of J&K on priority basis. The Central Government has invested so much in Kashmir in the past over seven years in development and connectivity projects but there are few areas where dialogue with people is a must. Delhi knows the issues. As for Pakistan is concerned, the neighbouring country is an epicenter of cross-border terrorism, but its people need to be convinced that this country is not against them. For that windows will have to be opened, how that can be done, no one should know it better than Delhi.

stories.headline: Army organises first-ever Gujjar and Bakarwal outreach programme in Wadder, Handwara
stories.title: Army organises first-ever Gujjar and Bakarwal outreach programme in Wadder, Handwara
stories.summary: Handwara, Nov 2: In a significant initiative aimed at promoting community engagement and strengthening ties with local residents, a Rashtriya Rifles unit organised a special outreach programme for the Gujjar and Bakarwal communities in the Wadder Rajwar area of Handwara for the first time. The programme witnessed enthusiastic participation from members of the local community and featured a series of cultural, recreational and sports activities designed to encourage community bonding and celebrate the rich cultural heritage of the Gujjar and Bakarwal communities. Various activities, including a Gojri singing competition, tug of war, jalebi jump, lemon race and sack race, were organised as part of the programme. These activities provided an opportunity for local residents, particularly youth and children, to showcase their talent and participate in a spirit of enthusiasm and camaraderie. A free medical camp was also organised during the event, providing medical assistance to members of the Gujjar and Bakarwal communities. Locals warmly appreciated the initiative taken by the Indian Army, describing it as a meaningful effort to reach out to the community and promote mutual understanding and goodwill. They also expressed gratitude to 21 Rashtriya Rifles for organising the programme and requested the Army to make such outreach activities an annual feature in Wadder Rajwar. The programme concluded with appreciation from community members, who termed the initiative a positive step towards strengthening the bond between the Indian Army and the local population.

stories.headline: POWERGRID: What strong oversight looks like
stories.title: POWERGRID: What strong oversight looks like
stories.summary: Every Kashmiri who has watched a 400 kV tower rise on a hillside, through an orchard or across a village path has seen how large these projects are. Many have also wondered how a project of this scale is governed. Power Grid Corporation of India Limited (POWERGRID) is a Maharatna public sector company and the backbone of the national transmission network. It carries our hydropower out in summer and brings in power when winter demand outstrips local generation. It also shapes where lines run, which trees are felled and how landowners are compensated. I write as an environmental scientist, a former regulator and a certified Independent Director. This author appreciates the work of POWERGRID’s engineers and linemen, who operate in some of the hardest terrain in the country. But at the same a, governance question comes to mind. What should independent oversight of a company like this look like? How closely does the public record show it, especially for Jammu & Kashmir? A strong company The starting point is a company that performs. According to PSU Connect’s report on its FY26 results, POWERGRID earned standalone net profit of ₹15,921 crore for 2025-26 and is paying a total dividend of ₹9 per share. Its own Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 records record capital expenditure of ₹39,967 crore, and PSU Watch’s report on the 37th annual general meeting says the company operates 292 substations and about 1.87 lakh circuit km of lines, with availability above 99.8%. The company’s Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) for 2025-26 says its core indicators carry reasonable assurance from TÜV India, a higher standard than many listed companies meet. The same report says Scope 1 and 2 emissions fell 17.95% in 2025-26 and that renewable reached 35.74% of its energy mix. These achievements are the base for any fair discussion. What the public registry shows, and what it cannot Most citizens would look first at the corporate registry. ZaubaCorp’s profile, compiled from Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) filings records POWERGRID’s Corporate Identification Number as L40101DL1989GOI038121, incorporation on 23 October 1989 as National Power Transmission Corporation Ltd, registration with the Registrar of Companies, Delhi, and classification as a Union government company. Authorised capital is ₹10,000 crore and paid-up capital ₹9,300.6 crore. It names directors including Ravisankar Ganesan, Ravindra Kumar Tyagi, Yatindra Dwivedi, Abhay Choudhary, Chetan Bansilal Kankariya, Saibaba Darbamulla, Lalit Bohra and Ram Naresh. The same page shows the limits of such aggregators. It lists the last annual general meeting as 30 August 2023 and the last balance sheet as 31 March 2023, although the notice of the 37th AGM confirms the company met on 20 August 2026. Assets, revenue and profit are blank, the member count reads zero and the complaints tables are empty. This is a lag in a third-party database, not evidence of any violation. It does mean that a citizen in Srinagar or Kishtwar who relies on it will learn little about how the board handles environmental and community risk. For that, the exchange filings, annual report and sustainability report are the better record. Independent oversight: why continuity matters The corporate governance filing that POWERGRID lodged with NSE for the quarter ended 31 March 2026 shows a board of ten with three independent directors, and records compliance with Regulation 17 of the SEBI Listing Regulations as “No”. The three, Rohit Vaswani, Shiv Tapasya Paswan and Smt. Sajal Jha, were appointed on 16 April and 16 May 2025. The company’s Annual Secretarial Compliance Report for 2025-26 explains that the board had no independent directors from November 2024, when two tenures ended, and that quorum could not always be met. The company’s stated position in both documents is that the President of India appoints independent directors through the Ministry of Power, and that it has repeatedly taken up the vacancies with the Ministry. The secretarial report adds that NSE and BSE each fined the company ₹14,39,600 for the March 2025 quarter and later waived the fines, on 12 September and 7 October 2025. The three directors have since completed their tenures. Scanx reported that Paswan and Vaswani finished on 15 April 2026, and a second Scanx headline says Jha’s tenure ended on 15 May 2026; each served about a year. I found no announcement of replacements. PSU Watch’s account of the 37th AGM on 20 August 2026 names only executives and a government nominee among the directors present. Market Screener’s board listing shows no independent director. I could not open the filing for the June 2026 quarter, so readers should check the company’s latest NSE and BSE announcements. If the position stands, it is a gap that belongs to the appointment process as much as to the company. The lesson is not about blame. The audit, nomination, stakeholder and risk committees all depend on independent members to function as designed, and short tenures and gaps make it hard to build the institutional memory that good oversight needs. The secretarial compliance report also notes that board-evaluation requirements were treated as not applicable under a 2017 MCA exemption for government companies. SEBI granted relief from Regulations 17(10) and 25(4) by a letter dated 2 March 2026. These are lawful accommodations. They do mean that the usual checks on directors apply more lightly to government companies, which makes the voluntary quality of governance more important. Who owns sustainability? In the documents I could read, there is no board committee or independent director with an ESG or sustainability mandate. The FY2025-26 BRSR names Naveen Srivastava, Director (Operations), as the highest authority for the business responsibility policy and the decision-maker on sustainability issues, with Vibhay Kumar, Executive Director (ESG & Net Zero), as the contact. The NSE governance filing lists the Audit, Nomination and Remuneration, Stakeholders Relationship and Risk Management committees, with an executive director chairing risk. The annual report describes a four-tier ESG structure, although the extract I read did not give its detail. Executive ownership of sustainability is sensible. Adding an independent chair for a sustainability committee would give the board a second line of oversight, which is good practice for a company with POWERGRID’s footprint. What the law provides, and where it stops The Companies Act 2013 is stronger than many assume. Section 166(2) asks every director to act in good faith for the company, its employees, shareholders and community, and for the protection of the environment. Section 149 and Schedule IV define the independent director’s role and Section 135 governs corporate social responsibility. These are duties of conduct, enforced by shareholders and regulators. A landowner cannot invoke them directly. The structure of the group adds another layer. Much newer transmission is built in single-project special purpose companies. Under Rule 4 of the Companies (Appointment and Qualification of Directors) Rules, as amended in 2017, unlisted wholly owned subsidiaries, joint ventures and dormant companies need not appoint independent directors. Regulation 24 of the SEBI Listing Regulations requires a listed parent to place at least one of its independent directors on an unlisted material subsidiary. opening: Every Kashmiri who has watched a 400 kV tower rise on a hillside, through an orchard or across a village path has seen how large these projects are.
Many have also wondered how a project of this scale is governed.
body: Power Grid Corporation of India Limited (POWERGRID) is a Maharatna public sector company and the backbone of the national transmission network.
It carries our hydropower out in summer and brings in power when winter demand outstrips local generation.
It also shapes where lines run, which trees are felled and how landowners are compensated.
I write as an environmental scientist, a former regulator and a certified Independent Director.
This author appreciates the work of POWERGRID’s engineers and linemen, who operate in some of the hardest terrain in the country.
But at the same a, governance question comes to mind.
What should independent oversight of a company like this look like?
How closely does the public record show it, especially for Jammu & Kashmir?
A strong company.
The starting point is a company that performs.
According to PSU Connect’s report on its FY26 results, POWERGRID earned standalone net profit of ₹15,921 crore for 2025-26 and is paying a total dividend of ₹9 per share.

Its own Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 records record capital expenditure of ₹39,967 crore, and PSU Watch’s report on the 37th annual general meeting says the company operates 292 substations and about 1.87 lakh circuit km of lines, with availability above 99.8%.

The company’s Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) for 2025-26 says its core indicators carry reasonable assurance from TÜV India, a higher standard than many listed companies meet.
The same report says Scope 1 and 2 emissions fell 17.95% in 2025-26 and that renewable reached 35.74% of its energy mix.
These achievements are the base for any fair discussion.
What the public registry shows, and what it cannot.
Most citizens would look first at the corporate registry.
Zauba.

Corp’s profile, compiled from Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) filings records POWERGRID’s Corporate Identification Number as L40101DL1989GOI038121, incorporation on 23 October 1989 as National Power Transmission Corporation Ltd, registration with the Registrar of Companies, Delhi, and classification as a Union government company.
Authorised capital is ₹10,000 crore and paid-up capital ₹9,300.6 crore.
It names directors including Ravisankar Ganesan, Ravindra Kumar Tyagi, Yatindra Dwivedi, Abhay Choudhary, Chetan Bansilal Kankariya, Saibaba Darbamulla, Lalit Bohra and Ram Naresh.
The same page shows the limits of such aggregators.
It lists the last annual general meeting as 30 August 2023 and the last balance sheet as 31 March 2023, although the notice of the 37th AGM confirms the company met on 20 August 2026.
Assets, revenue and profit are blank, the member count reads zero and the complaints tables are empty.
This is a lag in a third-party database, not evidence of any violation.
It does mean that a citizen in Srinagar or Kishtwar who relies on it will learn little about how the board handles environmental and community risk.
For that, the exchange filings, annual report and sustainability report are the better record.
Independent oversight: why continuity matters.

The three, Rohit Vaswani, Shiv Tapasya Paswan and Smt.
Sajal Jha, were appointed on 16 April and 16 May 2025.

The company’s Annual Secretarial Compliance Report for 2025-26 explains that the board had no independent directors from November 2024, when two tenures ended, and that quorum could not always be met.

The company’s stated position in both documents is that the President of India appoints independent directors through the Ministry of Power, and that it has repeatedly taken up the vacancies with the Ministry.
The secretarial report adds that NSE and BSE each fined the company ₹14,39,600 for the March 2025 quarter and later waived the fines, on 12 September and 7 October 2025.
The three directors have since completed their tenures.
Scanx reported that Paswan and Vaswani finished on 15 April 2026, and a second Scanx headline says Jha’s tenure ended on 15 May 2026; each served about a year.
I found no announcement of replacements.
PSU Watch’s account of the 37th AGM on 20 August 2026 names only executives and a government nominee among the directors present.
Market Screener’s board listing shows no independent director.
I could not open the filing for the June 2026 quarter, so readers should check the company’s latest NSE and BSE announcements.
If the position stands, it is a gap that belongs to the appointment process as much as to the company.
The lesson is not about blame.

The audit, nomination, stakeholder and risk committees all depend on independent members to function as designed, and short tenures and gaps make it hard to build the institutional memory that good oversight needs.
The secretarial compliance report also notes that board-evaluation requirements were treated as not applicable under a 2017 MCA exemption for government companies.
SEBI granted relief from Regulations 17(10) and 25(4) by a letter dated 2 March 2026.
These are lawful accommodations.
They do mean that the usual checks on directors apply more lightly to government companies, which makes the voluntary quality of governance more important.
Who owns sustainability?
In the documents.
I could read, there is no board committee or independent director with an ESG or sustainability mandate.

The FY2025-26 BRSR names Naveen Srivastava, Director (Operations), as the highest authority for the business responsibility policy and the decision-maker on sustainability issues, with Vibhay Kumar, Executive Director (ESG & Net Zero), as the contact.
The NSE governance filing lists the Audit, Nomination and Remuneration, Stakeholders Relationship and Risk Management committees, with an executive director chairing risk.
The annual report describes a four-tier ESG structure, although the extract.
I read did not give its detail.
Executive ownership of sustainability is sensible.
Adding an independent chair for a sustainability committee would give the board a second line of oversight, which is good practice for a company with POWERGRID’s footprint.
What the law provides, and where it stops.
The Companies Act 2013 is stronger than many assume.
Section 166(2) asks every director to act in good faith for the company, its employees, shareholders and community, and for the protection of the environment.
Section 149 and Schedule IV define the independent director’s role and Section 135 governs corporate social responsibility.
These are duties of conduct, enforced by shareholders and regulators.
A landowner cannot invoke them directly.
The structure of the group adds another layer.
Much newer transmission is built in single-project special purpose companies.

stories.headline: Ram Madhav arriving on day-long visit to Jammu today
stories.title: Ram Madhav arriving on day-long visit to Jammu today
stories.summary: Jammu, Nov 2: Amid ongoing political churning in J&K on different accounts, Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national vice president Ram Madhav is arriving in Jammu on a day-long visit tomorrow, November 3, 2026. The visit, which, according to the party, is aimed at holding only organisational meetings and deflating opposition-manufactured SIR controversy, has assumed significance, or more appropriately created flutter in the political corridors of J&K. In fact, political spins are being measured against his (Madhav’s) impressive past track-record vis-a-vis handling such politically tricky situations and carving “brighter opportunities” out of crisis or turbulence for the party as its (BJP's) point-man in J&K. J&K remembers him (Madhav) as the man, who made possible what used to be perceived as “impossible” –stitching BJP-PDP coalition to govern J&K in 2015 through “Agenda of Alliance” formulated along with Haseeb Drabu, former Finance Minister and the then senior PDP leader. But the J&K BJP unit dismisses all these angles as “rumour-mongering.” “He (Madhav) will be coming tomorrow morning. Initially there will be some party meetings. Later, he will be addressing media at 1 pm at BJP headquarter, Trikuta Nagar, Jammu,” shared J&K BJP chief spokesperson Sunil Sethi, while responding to Greater Kashmir queries about the central leader’s visit, his itinerary and major engagements. With regard to a question about the speculations linking Madhav’s visit to present spell of political upheaval in the UT amid chinks in National Conference's armour given open rebellion by its (NC's) veterans - post recent J&K cabinet expansion, Sethi dismissed such “spins” as “only conjectures.” “That is purely speculative. Presently there is no such effort. He is coming for the organisational meeting(s) followed by a press conference and addressing the concerns and clear deliberate confusion being created on Special Intensive Revision (SIR) (amid opposition propaganda). On SIR, the press conferences (by the party) are being held across the country – in different states and Union Territories (UTs). So that is all, one central leader is coming along with the state team,” Sethi said. “BJP national vice president is coming for that purpose. Rest is speculative that he is coming to form the government. He cannot comment upon that. There is no such thing, officially with us. Tomorrow’s visit is not related to anything like government formation or some political equations. There is nothing like that. It is a routine SIR-related press conference and organisational activities,” the J&K BJP chief spokesperson asserted. Will NC rebellion or evolving scenario post cabinet expansion be part of deliberations during J&K BJP organisational meetings with Madhav? “See, we are keenly watching what is happening in the National Conference. Presently there is no decision of making any move in this direction by the BJP. Even otherwise I don’t think so. These types of things will never be discussed in the organisational meetings. So there’s no need to see or read more than that (with regard to Madhav’s visit),” Sethi maintains. Nevertheless, it is not just BJP keenly watching developments unfolding in the NC, all political beings, including analysts in J&K or outside, are also earnestly following its (BJP’s) each and every move. Madhav was the party’s election in-charge for the 2024 J&K assembly polls. He was appointed national vice president earlier this year as part of the organisational team under party president Nitin Nabin. Interestingly, BJP national vice president’s Jammu visit will coincide with another significant political development unfolding in Srinagar on November 3, 2026 – the resignation of Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi - NC MP from Srinagar parliamentary constituency both from Lok Sabha as well as from party (NC). Just a coincidence, probably!

Interestingly, BJP national vice president’s Jammu visit will coincide with another significant political development unfolding in Srinagar on November 3, 2026 – the resignation of Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi - NC MP from Srinagar parliamentary constituency both from Lok Sabha as well as from party (NC).
